catalog: song-forms/english-forms.md, five data tables, 364 actual form rows; line numbers are one-based in the original
method: All 62 supplied labels, in original order, compared with catalog titles, aliases and structure descriptions. A related item or return device is not an automatic synonym. A missing umbrella, a whole form, an inner pattern, a tonal scheme, a performance convention and a scope question are recorded separately. External references adjudicate named distinctions; a bare catalog match is checked directly against its cited line(s). An empty citation list makes no independent repertory claim.

terms.detail: A module is a unit from which a form is assembled. The term alone specifies neither a sequence nor a complete lyric.
Rotation can describe a pass through a recurring series of sections. Hudson’s second verse–chorus rotation in “Master of Puppets” is a specific analysis; rotation by itself prescribes no song form.
A pass through a repeating unit is present in several rows. “Song cycle” on line 68 means an ordered collection of independent songs, a different scale and sense.
A passage’s role in its context is a classification dimension, not a whole-piece blueprint.
Opening and closing material frames a larger structure. A framing role does not determine what lies between the boundaries.
Initiating describes a beginning function. It can be assigned at several hierarchical levels without implying a fixed song type.
Medial describes a position or function between initiation and conclusion. Sections with different content can fulfill the role.
Concluding describes a local or global ending function; it does not prescribe a complete form.
Open Music Theory treats the chorus as the primary module in verse–chorus form and strophe as primary in AABA. The role depends on the form, so it does not create a new whole song.
Open Music Theory calls the verse a secondary module in verse–chorus form. That role within one analytical model is not a complete song structure.
Auxiliary describes noncore material in a form, such as an intro or coda. It belongs on a part or relation.
Loose describes the formal organization attributed to a verse. No fixed sectional template follows, and the catalog’s simple/contrasting distinction is about different properties.
terms.scope: An operational definition of looseness is needed before tagging individual songs.

terms.detail: Tight characterizes a chorus or contrast with a verse. It is independent of the underlying verse–chorus plan.
terms.scope: No English song row is established by the qualifier itself.

terms.detail: The statement–restatement–departure–conclusion model describes a commonly analyzed phrase or section organization. Nobile gives early Beatles examples. It can operate above that level, so retain the level of each instance.
terms.scope: Document and diagram as an internal schema. It is not automatically an additional whole song.

terms.detail: “Compound” specifies more than one level of grouping, not which groups. Compound AABA is a concrete problematic alias on line 32.
Same tune returns across successive verses; “form” adds no new entry.
The name matches directly. One or more musically altered strophes do not create another catalog identity.
The planner overview already names verse-chorus; multiple catalog entries specialize it, but none of the 364 catalog rows supplies a general selectable verse–chorus parent.
terms.scope: Catalog navigation gap; not an absent planner feature.

terms.detail: Covach’s simple-verse terminology denotes the repeating single-strophe layout here. Add a search synonym while retaining the scholarly distinction between repeating underlying harmony and literally identical melody.
The catalog uses Simple verse-chorus and defines shared underlying chords.
Same category as Contrasting verse-chorus.
The verse-refrain name is already the alias of Strophic with refrain. Line 34 uses a historically different “refrain” for the main section following an introductory verse.
Binary is named. Its repeat-sign and repeat-order disagreement is documented separately rather than counted as a missing form.
The ABA category is present under Ternary.
The catalog includes a central recurring section alternating with episodes and lists ABACA and ABACABA.
Arch already expresses the mirror arrangement.
Through-composition is named. The row’s “nothing repeats” is insufficient for published through-composed classes that share themes without repeating whole sections.

Spicer distinguishes building a groove through successive entries of its layers. This can organize an opening or section of a larger song. The cumulative lyrics in line 122 and persistence of one riff in line 81 do not imply this process. A texture may accumulate within an otherwise ordinary verse–chorus form.
terms.scope: Account for musical layers and time scale; lyrics alone cannot verify it.

terms.detail: The folk add-on-text meaning is present as Cumulative song. The music-theory meaning in Spicer and Burkholder concerns earlier fragments coming together in a later thematic culmination; it is a distinct process.
terms.scope: Represent both explicitly; do not add a duplicate for the folk sense.

terms.detail: Osborn identifies a new, thematically independent climax heard only at the end, following an earlier expectation established by the song. A last louder chorus is insufficient. His study distinguishes two-part, three-part and extended designs.
terms.scope: Strong specific English-language song candidate.

terms.detail: Nobile calls this the telos principle. It models directed section functions over a verse–prechorus–chorus cycle, including subversions; it is not a synonym of Osborn’s once-only terminal climax.

Sonata-allegro has its own formal sense, but this comparison has not documented an English-text vocal example and an appropriate representation of tonal functions. Do not count the omission as an English lyric form on name alone.
terms.scope: Wider musical form; candidate for a separate, sourced vocal repertoire check.

terms.detail: Spelled-out and numeral names denote the same twelve-bar entry.
Spelled-out and numeral names denote the same sixteen-bar entry.
Spelled-out and numeral names denote the same eight-bar entry.

The named family is based on the chord changes to Gershwin’s “I Got Rhythm”. AABA is a sectional outline shared by unrelated tunes, while line 54’s new words on an existing tune represent a different reuse mechanism.
terms.scope: Ground it as a harmonic schema and preserve the distinction between a jazz contrafact and a new text set to an existing tune.

terms.detail: Both Stollen and the contrasting Abgesang are named by the existing entry.

The ritornello that recurs between solo entries is audible and identified by exact listening times in Handel’s English-text “Every Valley.” The alias ritornello on Stornello denotes a different three-line verse type.
terms.scope: English vocal evidence exists; represent the recurring orchestral material and vocal episodes, which may belong inside a larger aria.

terms.detail: Da capo is a return-to-the-beginning direction. Its aria realization already has a named entry; “da capo” in isolation is not another song type.
The segno is a notational reference point for navigation; it does not specify a complete arrangement.
The coda sign is a navigation marker. A coda section and the sign itself are different objects.

Vuelta can designate a return or a part in a tradition-specific stanza/refrain structure. The label alone does not identify which tradition, complete form, or English-language realization was intended.
terms.scope: Require a score or performer edition and identification of the language and structural level.

terms.detail: Copla–estribillo describes a possible stanza/refrain relationship; a translated gloss alone cannot identify it with every English verse–refrain example or specify the ordering of a particular traditional realization.
terms.scope: A concrete English-text setting and a specialist source for the intended tradition remain to be checked.

terms.detail: Cuban son can move into a responsive montuno section; the generic Call-and-response row covers a relationship but not the son design. “Son montuno” also names a style.
terms.scope: This inquiry did not verify an English-text example with an unambiguous complete design.

terms.detail: Kirtan describes a devotional performance tradition. A documented Padavali Kirtan recording identifies a specific regional practice; repeating a response alone cannot establish one invariant song plan for all kirtan.
terms.scope: Verify a particular subform and English-text setting independently.

terms.detail: Qawwali is a Sufi musical tradition and performance practice. The award documentation recognizes its practitioners; it supplies no universal ordered section grammar for English lyrics.
terms.scope: Specific repertoire and performance segmentation are required.

terms.detail: Gharana indicates an artistic lineage or school. Multiple forms may circulate within a gharana, so no whole-song diagram follows.
Sthayi and antara identify two compositional sections in North Indian practice. Treat the two-part organization on its own terms, not as an automatic alias for the catalog’s Western Binary row.
terms.scope: An English-language work and a tradition-specific delineation of the repeat/return remain unverified.

terms.detail: Darbar describes pallavi, an optional anupallavi, and charanam in a kriti. A source-attested sectional design is present, but English-text eligibility has not been verified in this pass.
terms.scope: Retain the optional middle section; do not assert all compositions or repertoires follow the full three-part pattern.

terms.detail: A bandish is a fixed composition in Hindustani practice. The category can supply material for elaboration, but by itself fixes neither all larger performance sections nor an English-language text.
terms.scope: Verify the compositional subtype, structure and language of a concrete example.

terms.detail: Jor is a pulsed phase of an instrumental raga presentation; a performance stage alone is not a missing English lyric form.
Jhala is a fast climactic phase typically discussed in instrumental performance. Treat it at the performance-section level.
A gat is a fixed instrumental composition in the raga tradition. It can anchor improvisation, but a textless gat supplies no lyric sequence.
Tihai is a rhythmic pattern articulated three times to produce an arrival. Its scale can vary. It is a cadential device rather than an independent English lyric form.

Head–solos–head appears as an alias and as the catalog example, so the musical sequence has already been discussed. It needs its own conceptual identity: a head arrangement concerns how the players devise and remember an arrangement.
terms.scope: Jazz performance envelope distinct from the form of the tune played inside one chorus.

terms.detail: “Changes” are the chord progression used while improvising. Playing over the changes neither requires a specific length nor identifies a distinct whole-song scheme.

The catalog already includes loops serving rap, groove-based songs, rounds and ostinato chants. The time unit, material repeated and role at the song level determine whether two instances share a form.
terms.scope: Useful process/facet; one new template for every possible loop would be unsound.

terms.detail: “Track form” does not identify one ordered schema, theorist, recording or decision rule here. No concrete addition is warranted from the phrase alone.
These entries involve simultaneous materials, riffs and chants over ostinati. Layering alone neither dictates the entry order nor guarantees Spicer’s accumulative technique.
Adding lyrics in a chain is already represented, as is the more general possibility of layers accruing in music theory. “Additive” can also refer to rhythm. Identify what is added and at what scale.

Dropping successive layers is a plausible process, but this inventory gives no named canonical vocal form, exact decrement, or qualifying English example; do not infer one by reversing an accumulative diagram.
“Beat-driven” distinguishes multiple arrangements by musical emphasis rather than by a sequence of sections. The catalog already has several different beat-centered examples.
